Figure 4 shows the working port design at the top of the tank that seals against the outer shell and provides for charging and discharging the inner tank. The outer shell is split into two halves at its midline, allowing for insertion of the seal cap with an O-ring that contacts the inner surface of the shell for sealing the vacuum space. A bearing nut on the outside is threaded onto the cap to compress the seal against the shell. With this location predicted to be significantly warmer than the inner tank and air being the working fluid, standard O-ring material options may be expected to provide effective sealing. Hydrogen ingress and egress to the tank is performed through a tube-within-a-tube arrangement. The inner tube transitions from stainless steel to a PTFE section extending to the bottom of the tank, allowing for hydrogen withdrawal with minimal heat conduction. The outer stainless steel tube passes through the inner tank upper bulkhead via a Swagelok FK tube fitting (commonly used in hydrogen piping) welded to the bulkhead. Just above the fitting this tube incorporates a flexible bellows section to compensate for small misalignments and thermal motion while avoiding the transfer of loads from the port and exterior tubing to the inner tank, potentially compromising the inner tank seal. Above the bellows section, the tube is welded to a larger flanged cylindrical piece that is loaded against the upper inner surface of the cap to seal and support the external tubing. A metal C-seal is targeted for this location, where the metal-to-metal interface is favorable to conventional seals but at a temperature that is expected to be outside of the limits of common O-ring materials. Shell flange and inner tank support The outer shell is split at its midline, with metal flanges bonded to each end and bolted around the inner tank at assembly. An O-ring between the flanges seals the vacuum space. The support consists of a single ring at the midsection of the tank, bonded to the inner tank and interfacing with the flanges of the outer shell halves. The support may be metal or composite, with material selection a balance between structural and thermal performance. Locating the support at the tank midline offers a number of advantages versus placement at the top and bottom. Attempting to hold the tank with top and bottom supports creates issues with proper alignment and load balancing between the two end supports, and so would be unforgiving of geometrical variance and relative thermal motion. The midline support has no such issues, with small variations accommodated by the bellows tube at the port. Further, the midline support allows for full coverage of MLI around the inner tank and is assembled with visibility to how the components and MLI are seated. 1.3.
